q: Under DPWH Item 405, what maximum water-cement ratio applies to Class P concrete?
ref: DPWH Standard Specifications (Blue Book), Item 405 Table 405.1 Composition and Strength of Concrete
n: Class P: 440 kg/m³ (11 bags) cement, w/c 0.49, slump 100 mm maximum, coarse aggregate 19.0–4.75 mm, f'c 37.7 MPa. Class P is the high-strength mix for prestressed concrete, with the lowest water-cement ratio and the most cement.

q: What do sprinkling and fog spraying do when curing concrete?
o: They seal the surface so no water can escape
They keep the surface wet, replacing water lost to evaporation
They heat the concrete to speed up setting
ref: ACI 308R Guide to curing concrete
n: Water-adding methods (ponding, sprinkling, fogging, wet coverings) supply water to the surface. Water-retaining methods (plastic sheets, waterproof paper, curing compounds) stop the concrete's own water from escaping.

q: Under DPWH Item 405, what minimum cement content applies to Class A concrete?
ref: DPWH Standard Specifications (Blue Book), Item 405 Table 405.1 Composition and Strength of Concrete
n: Class A: 364 kg/m³ (9.1 bags) cement, w/c 0.53, slump 50–100 mm, coarse aggregate 37.5–4.75 mm, f'c 20.7 MPa. Class A is the general structural class for footings, columns, beams, slabs and bridge superstructures.

q: What guides the choice of maximum aggregate size for a concrete mix?
o: Always use the smallest size available
Use any size, since it does not affect the mix
Use the largest economical size that fits the member dimensions and bar spacing
ref: NSCP 2015 Sec. 426.4.2.1 (ACI 318-14 26.4.2.1) Aggregate size limits
n: Larger, well-graded aggregate has fewer voids, so it needs less cement paste. It must still pass between bars and fill the forms, which sets the upper limits.

q: Under DPWH Item 405, what percentage of fine aggregate must pass the 4.75 mm (No. 4) sieve?
ref: DPWH Standard Specifications, Item 405.2.3 Fine aggregate grading and deleterious limits
n: Nearly all fine aggregate passes the No. 4 sieve; that sieve is the dividing line between fine and coarse aggregate.

q: Under DPWH Item 405, what slump applies to Class B concrete?
ref: DPWH Standard Specifications (Blue Book), Item 405 Table 405.1 Composition and Strength of Concrete
n: Class B: 320 kg/m³ (8 bags) cement, w/c 0.58, slump 50–100 mm, coarse aggregate 50–4.75 mm, f'c 16.5 MPa. Class B is a leaner mix for massive or lightly reinforced work, such as gravity walls and footings of small structures.

q: Bars in a beam are 40 mm apart clear. What is the largest nominal aggregate size allowed by the bar spacing?
ref: NSCP 2015 Sec. 426.4.2.1 (ACI 318-14 26.4.2.1) Aggregate size limits
n: Aggregate may not exceed three-fourths of the minimum clear spacing between bars: ¾ × 40 = 30 mm.

q: Under DPWH Item 405, what maximum water-cement ratio applies to Class B concrete?
ref: DPWH Standard Specifications (Blue Book), Item 405 Table 405.1 Composition and Strength of Concrete
n: Class B: 320 kg/m³ (8 bags) cement, w/c 0.58, slump 50–100 mm, coarse aggregate 50–4.75 mm, f'c 16.5 MPa. Class B is a leaner mix for massive or lightly reinforced work, such as gravity walls and footings of small structures.

q: Which curing method keeps a layer of water standing on the concrete surface?
ref: ACI 308R Guide to curing concrete
n: Ponding floods a flat slab behind small earth or sand dikes. It is very effective for slabs and pavements but only works on level surfaces.

q: Why is beach sand not allowed in concrete without the engineer's approval?
o: Its salt (chlorides) corrodes the reinforcement, and its grains are often uniform and rounded
ref: DPWH Standard Specifications, Item 405
n: Chlorides from seawater attack steel bars and cause efflorescence. Beach sand is also often poorly graded. It can be used only if washed and tested, with approval.

q: Above about what temperature should concrete be kept during curing so that hydration continues well?
ref: ACI 308R Guide to curing concrete
n: Hydration slows sharply below about 10°C and stops near freezing. Very high temperatures also harm long-term strength, so curing aims for moderate, steady warmth.

q: Under DPWH Item 405, what maximum water-cement ratio applies to Class C concrete?
ref: DPWH Standard Specifications (Blue Book), Item 405 Table 405.1 Composition and Strength of Concrete
n: Class C: 380 kg/m³ (9.5 bags) cement, w/c 0.55, slump 50–100 mm, coarse aggregate 12.5–4.75 mm, f'c 20.7 MPa. Class C uses small (12.5 mm) coarse aggregate for thin, heavily reinforced sections such as railings and thin slabs.

q: Under DPWH Item 405, what percentage of fine aggregate must pass the 1.18 mm (No. 16) sieve?
ref: DPWH Standard Specifications, Item 405.2.3 Fine aggregate grading and deleterious limits
n: The middle sieves set the sand's grading. A well-graded sand fills the voids between gravel particles with less cement paste.

q: Under DPWH Item 405, what minimum 28-day cylinder strength applies to Class C concrete?
ref: DPWH Standard Specifications (Blue Book), Item 405 Table 405.1 Composition and Strength of Concrete
n: Class C: 380 kg/m³ (9.5 bags) cement, w/c 0.55, slump 50–100 mm, coarse aggregate 12.5–4.75 mm, f'c 20.7 MPa. Class C uses small (12.5 mm) coarse aggregate for thin, heavily reinforced sections such as railings and thin slabs.

n: Seal concrete: 380 kg/m³ (9.5 bags) cement, w/c 0.58, slump 100–200 mm, coarse aggregate 25–4.75 mm, f'c 20.7 MPa. Seal concrete is placed under water to seal cofferdams, so it must flow (100–200 mm slump) and has extra cement to make up for washout.

q: Under DPWH Item 405, what is the maximum amount of clay lumps or shale allowed in fine aggregate?
ref: DPWH Standard Specifications, Item 405.2.3 Fine aggregate grading and deleterious limits
n: Clay lumps and soft shale break down in the mix, weaken the paste and cause pop-outs, so they are held to 1% by mass.

q: Why may different sources of fine aggregate not be mixed or alternated in the same class of concrete without approval?
o: Changing sources changes the grading and water demand, so the concrete becomes inconsistent
Because all sand is the same
Because it is illegal to buy sand from two suppliers
ref: DPWH Standard Specifications, Item 405.2.3 Fine aggregate grading and deleterious limits
n: Each sand has its own grading, shape and fines. Switching without adjusting the mix changes slump, strength and color from batch to batch.

q: Which of these is an admixture?
o: A water-reducing agent added during mixing
ref: ACI CT-13 Concrete terminology
n: An admixture is any material other than water, aggregate and hydraulic cement that is added before or during mixing to change the concrete's properties.

q: Under DPWH Item 405, what minimum cement content applies to seal concrete?
ref: DPWH Standard Specifications (Blue Book), Item 405 Table 405.1 Composition and Strength of Concrete
n: Seal concrete: 380 kg/m³ (9.5 bags) cement, w/c 0.58, slump 100–200 mm, coarse aggregate 25–4.75 mm, f'c 20.7 MPa. Seal concrete is placed under water to seal cofferdams, so it must flow (100–200 mm slump) and has extra cement to make up for washout.

q: Which of these is a wet-covering method of curing?
o: Wet burlap kept damp over the concrete
ref: ACI 308R Guide to curing concrete
n: Wet burlap, wet sand, wet earth, sawdust or straw supply water and must be kept continuously damp. If they dry out they can draw water from the concrete.

q: Under DPWH Item 405, what is the maximum amount of fine aggregate that may pass the 0.075 mm (No. 200) sieve by washing?
ref: DPWH Standard Specifications, Item 405.2.3 Fine aggregate grading and deleterious limits
n: Material finer than 0.075 mm (silt and clay dust) coats the particles and raises the water demand, so it is limited to 3%.

q: Under DPWH Item 405, what percentage of fine aggregate must pass the 0.150 mm (No. 100) sieve?
ref: DPWH Standard Specifications, Item 405.2.3 Fine aggregate grading and deleterious limits
n: Only a little very fine material is allowed; too much raises the water demand and shrinkage.

q: Which admixture delays the setting of concrete, for example in hot weather or long hauls?
ref: ASTM C494 Type B
n: Retarders (ASTM C494 Type B) slow the start of setting so concrete stays workable longer and cold joints are avoided.

q: Under DPWH Item 405, what coarse aggregate grading (size range) applies to Class B concrete?
ref: DPWH Standard Specifications (Blue Book), Item 405 Table 405.1 Composition and Strength of Concrete
n: Class B: 320 kg/m³ (8 bags) cement, w/c 0.58, slump 50–100 mm, coarse aggregate 50–4.75 mm, f'c 16.5 MPa. Class B is a leaner mix for massive or lightly reinforced work, such as gravity walls and footings of small structures.

q: Why does well-graded, larger aggregate usually save cement?
o: It has fewer voids, so less cement paste is needed to fill them
It reacts with cement to make it stronger
ref: NSCP 2015 Sec. 426.4.2.1 (ACI 318-14 26.4.2.1) Aggregate size limits
n: Paste must fill every void and coat every particle. Larger, well-graded aggregate has less surface area and fewer voids, so the same strength needs less paste.

q: How is concrete best described?
o: A mixture of lime and sand only
An artificial stone made of cement, fine aggregate, coarse aggregate and water, with or without admixtures
A mixture of cement and water only
ref: ACI CT-13 Concrete terminology
n: Cement and water form a paste that hardens and binds the aggregates into a stone-like mass. Cement and water alone are neat paste; lime and sand make mortar.

q: Which curing method works by keeping the concrete's own water from evaporating, rather than adding water?
ref: ACI 308R Guide to curing concrete
n: Curing compounds, plastic sheeting and waterproof paper seal the surface. They suit places where keeping the concrete wet is hard, such as walls and high-rise slabs.

q: For how long is concrete usually moist-cured?
o: About 7 days for ordinary cement, and longer for slow-gaining mixes
ref: ACI 308R Guide to curing concrete
n: Ordinary portland cement concrete is commonly cured for at least 7 days (3 days for high-early-strength cement, up to 14 days for blended or mass concrete). The specification sets the actual period.

q: A slab is 150 mm thick. What is the largest nominal aggregate size allowed by the slab depth?
ref: NSCP 2015 Sec. 426.4.2.1 (ACI 318-14 26.4.2.1) Aggregate size limits
n: Aggregate may not exceed one-third of the slab depth: 150 / 3 = 50 mm. The bar spacing may still set a smaller limit.

q: Which ingredient of concrete usually costs the most per cubic metre of concrete?
ref: DPWH Blue Book Item 405
n: Aggregates are the largest part by volume but cheap. Cement is a small part by volume but costly, so reducing cement (with good grading and larger aggregate) cuts cost.

q: Which of these may be used as coarse aggregate in DPWH concrete?
o: Crushed clay brick with plaster attached
Crushed stone, gravel or blast-furnace slag that is hard, strong and clean
ref: DPWH Standard Specifications, Item 405
n: Coarse aggregate must be hard, strong, durable and free of adherent coatings, organic matter and salt. Crushed stone, gravel and air-cooled slag qualify.

q: In a typical normal-strength concrete, roughly what share of the volume is cement?
ref: DPWH Blue Book Item 405
n: By volume, aggregates are about 60 to 75% (gravel the largest part), water about 15 to 20% and cement about 10 to 15%.

q: Which admixture speeds up setting and early hardening?
ref: ASTM C494 Type C
n: Accelerators (ASTM C494 Type C) shorten setting time and raise early strength, helpful for early form removal. Chloride types are not allowed near prestressing steel.

q: Above about what internal relative humidity should concrete be kept for hydration to continue?
ref: ACI 308R Guide to curing concrete
n: Below about 80% relative humidity inside the concrete, hydration slows greatly. Curing keeps the concrete moist enough for the cement to keep reacting.

q: A pour needs 6 m³ of Class A concrete. Using 364 kg of cement per m³ and 40 kg bags, about how many bags are needed?
ref: DPWH Standard Specifications (Blue Book), Item 405 Table 405.1 Composition and Strength of Concrete
n: 6 × 364 = 2,184 kg of cement. 2,184 / 40 = 54.6, so order about 55 bags.

q: What does curing concrete mean?
o: Letting the concrete dry out as fast as possible
Adding water to fresh concrete to raise its slump
Keeping enough moisture and warmth for long enough so the concrete gains its intended properties
ref: ACI 308R Guide to curing concrete
n: Curing is about moisture, temperature and time. Concrete that dries too early can lose much of its potential strength and develop surface cracks.

q: Under DPWH Item 405, what percentage of fine aggregate must pass the 0.300 mm (No. 50) sieve?
ref: DPWH Standard Specifications, Item 405.2.3 Fine aggregate grading and deleterious limits
n: 5 to 30% passing the No. 50 sieve keeps enough fines for workability without making the mix sticky.

q: Under DPWH Item 405, what is the basis for counting cement bags per cubic metre?

n: Philippine cement is sold in 40 kg bags, so the table's bag counts (for example 9.1 bags for 364 kg) divide the cement content by 40. The 94 lb bag is the American size.

o: Natural sand or stone screenings with hard, strong, durable particles

n: Fine aggregate may be natural sand, stone screenings or similar approved inert material, clean and free of clay, organic matter and salt.

q: Under DPWH Item 405, how close must the measured cement content be to the design cement content?
o: Any amount, if strength is met
ref: DPWH Standard Specifications (Blue Book), Item 405 Table 405.1 Composition and Strength of Concrete
n: The table allows the measured cement content to vary by no more than 2% by mass from the design value, so batching must be accurate.

q: A wall form is 200 mm wide. What is the largest nominal aggregate size allowed by the form width?
ref: NSCP 2015 Sec. 426.4.2.1 (ACI 318-14 26.4.2.1) Aggregate size limits
n: Aggregate may not exceed one-fifth of the narrowest form dimension: 200 / 5 = 40 mm.

q: Under DPWH Item 405, what percentage of fine aggregate must pass the 9.5 mm sieve?

q: Why is concrete cured for several days instead of a few hours?
o: Hydration continues for days, and strength depends on moisture being present all that time
Concrete sets in minutes and needs nothing after
ref: ACI 308R Guide to curing concrete
n: Strength keeps growing as long as water and cement keep reacting. Concrete cured 7 days moist is much stronger at 28 days than concrete left to dry after one day.
